opus-5.5.text:
I think open source is one of the most rewarding things a university researcher or student can do, and honestly it's been central to my own path. When I started working on things like XGBoost, and later TVM and MLC, I wasn't thinking of it as a separate activity from research. It was a way of making the research real.

In academia we usually measure impact through papers, and papers are important. But a paper describes an idea; open source lets people actually use that idea. When someone on the other side of the world downloads your code, runs it on their own problem, and it works, or even when it breaks and they file an issue, that's a very direct kind of feedback you don't get from reviewers. It tells you what really matters and what doesn't, and that often pushes the research in better directions.

For students especially, I think it teaches things that are hard to learn otherwise. You learn to write code that other people can read and build on. You learn to think about design, about abstractions that will survive contact with real use cases. And you learn to communicate: writing documentation, answering questions, reviewing contributions. Those skills compound over a career, whether you stay in academia or go to industry.

There's also a community aspect. Open source lets a small university group collaborate with people at companies, at other universities, with independent developers, and that network becomes bigger than any single lab. Some of the best collaborators I've had came from people who first showed up as contributors.

That said, I'd be honest that it takes real effort. Maintaining a project is not glamorous; a lot of it is fixing bugs, handling releases, keeping things compatible. The academic incentive system doesn't always reward that directly. So my advice is to be intentional: pick problems where having a usable system actually amplifies the research, build something you yourself want to use, and treat the users as part of the research loop. If you do that, open source isn't a distraction from research. It becomes one of the strongest ways to do research that has lasting impact.

r001.rationale: It says open source makes research ideas usable, describing people downloading and running the code on their own problems.

r002.rationale: It discusses skills students gain in design and writing code, but does not say participation expands PhD students’ opportunities to architect large systems from scratch.

r003.rationale: It describes collaboration across universities, companies, and independent developers, but does not identify universities’ relative neutrality as conducive to open-source work.

r004.rationale: It notes that maintenance involves bugs, releases, and compatibility, and says the academic incentive system does not directly reward that work; it also contrasts research impact measured through papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think open source is one of the best things a university researcher or student can do, and I say that from experience, because almost everything in my own career came out of it.

When I was a PhD student I built XGBoost, and later MXNet and TVM, and none of those started as grand plans. They started as tools I needed for my own research. The thing that changed everything was putting them out there. The moment real people start using your code, you get a kind of feedback that you never get from a paper review. Someone from a company tells you it breaks on their data. Someone on Kaggle finds a trick that makes it faster. Suddenly your research problem is grounded in reality, and that makes the research better, not worse.

For students specifically, I think open source teaches things a classroom cannot. You learn to write code that other people can read and maintain. You learn to communicate, to write documentation, to argue about design in a pull request, to handle criticism. And you learn to build a community, which is really about trust. Those are skills that matter whether you stay in academia or go to industry.

There is also a fairness aspect. A lot of the most important infrastructure in machine learning, the compilers, the training frameworks, the serving systems, requires a large collective effort that no single lab or student can do alone. Open source is how academia can still participate in that and have real impact, even without the resources of a big company. If your work only lives in a paper, it has a shelf life of maybe a year. If it lives in a project that people depend on, it can keep compounding for a decade.

Now, I will be honest that there is tension with the traditional incentive system. Maintaining a project does not always count toward a thesis or a tenure case the way a publication does. So my advice to students is to be deliberate. Pick problems where the research question and the useful artifact are the same thing, so that building the system is the research. And work with advisors who understand that. I have been lucky in that regard, and I try to create the same environment for my own students at CMU now.

So overall, I view it not as a side activity but as a core part of how research should be done in this field. The best research is research that people can actually run.

r001.rationale: It says that releasing code lets real people use it, grounding research in practical problems and making the work more impactful.

r002.rationale: It discusses skills students gain and collective infrastructure work, but does not say open source expands students’ opportunities to architect large systems from scratch.

r003.rationale: It says open source lets academia participate despite limited resources, but does not identify universities’ relative neutrality as conducive to this work.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says project maintenance may not count toward a thesis or tenure case as publications do.

astra-6.text:
I think open source is a very natural activity for university researchers and students, because research is about creating knowledge and sharing it with others. A paper communicates an idea, but an open-source project allows people to actually try that idea, understand how it works, and build on top of it.

For students, it’s also a great learning experience. When someone else uses your code, you start to see questions that you might not encounter in a research prototype. Is it easy to use? Does it work in a different setting? Can someone else contribute? Those questions can improve the software, but they can also lead to new research directions.

Of course, maintaining a project takes time, so I don’t think every research project needs to become a widely used software system. But I see open source as a way to connect research with a broader community, where people learn from one another and work together to make the ideas more useful.

r001.rationale: It says open source lets people try research ideas, build on them, and make them more useful, connecting research with practical use.

r002.rationale: It does not mention PhD students or expanded opportunities to architect large systems from scratch.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss universities’ neutrality.

r004.rationale: It notes that maintenance takes time, but does not say this work is mismatched with activities traditionally counted as research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open source is a very natural activity for university researchers and students, because research is about creating knowledge and sharing it. A paper communicates the ideas, while an open-source project lets other people try those ideas, build on them, and discover things you didn’t anticipate.

For students, it’s also a great learning opportunity. You learn how to work with other people, explain your design decisions, and understand problems that come from actual users. Those interactions can lead to interesting research questions.

Of course, releasing code is only the beginning. Building a useful project takes maintenance, documentation, and a community where people feel comfortable contributing. I think that work is valuable alongside publishing papers, because it helps research have a lasting impact.

r003.rationale: Does not mention universities’ neutrality or connect it to open-source work.
